To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ingestion of 12. 5 g FOS per day in healthy humans led to an increase of colonic bifid bacteria but did not affect the concentrations of fecal bile acids or neutral sterols or the activities of nitoreductase, azo-reductase and beta-glucurono-nidase.
fructo- oligosaccharides increase fecal bifid bacteria in humans but have no effect on fecal nitroreductases, azoreductases, beta-glucuronides, bile acids, neutral sterols or fecal pH.
fructo- oligosaccharides, at a dose of 12 g/day, increase fecal bifidogenic flora in humans but do not significantly alter other metabolic indexes of colon cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of a dietary fiber (fructo-oligo-saccharide) on fecal bifido-bacteria and selected metabolic indices of colonic carcinogenesis in healthy human subjects.
the potential role of FOS as prebiotic food supplements in cancer prevention.
the effect of a dietary supplement on the fecal microflora and some factors that may be involved in the pathophysiology of colonic cancer in humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of FOS on the colonic microbiota and metabolism in humans remains to be established and that further research is needed.
FOS ingestion in the doses tested does not seem to exert a protective effect on colon carcinogenesis.
the effects of FFS on colonic cancer are not yet clear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FOS are not a cancer preventive agent.
fructo- oligosaccharide ingestion at a dose of 12,5 g/d for 12 days in healthy humans does not lead to beneficial changes in the metabolic indexes of colon cancer.
the ingestion of 12. 5 g FOS/day in healthy humans does not affect the colonic environment and does not modify the fecal concentrations of potentially carcinogenic compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ingestion of FOS in humans does not seem to have any significant effect on selected metabolic indexes of colonic carcinogenesis in healthy volunteers.
FOS ingestion does not appear to be a useful dietary strategy for the prevention of colonic cancer, at least in the short term.
the consumption of FOS does not seem to have an impact on the metabolic indices we studied.
